item.title: Molecular pendulum shuttles protons to enable rapid hydrogen production in enzymes
item.description: Nearly all metabolic processes require protons—positively charged hydrogen atoms. Although these are abundant in the cellular fluid, the biocatalysts involved depend on mechanisms for efficiently capturing protons and transporting them to the site where catalysis occurs. Enzymes from microorganisms can produce hydrogen (H₂) by combining electrons with protons. These so-called hydrogenases are so efficient that one biocatalyst can capture nearly 10,000 protons per second. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan to launch world-first mission to moon of Mars
item.description: Japanese scientists will launch a spacecraft on Tuesday that aims to be the first to retrieve samples from one of Mars' moons, potentially helping unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Improves Shock, Vibration Analysis
item.description: Rockets vibrate, shake, and flex intensely as they climb into space, and spacecraft packed with delicate scientific instruments must survive those forces. Before any rocket leaves the ground, NASA engineers work to predict how those stresses will affect every part of a spacecraft. To do that, engineers in the Dynamic Environments Group with NASA’s Launch […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Elyna Niles-Carnes

item.title: The housing gap between young people with and without wealthy parents has nearly doubled
item.description: Among 30-year-olds with parents in the wealthiest fifth of the population, nearly seven out of ten own their own home. Among those with parents in the least wealthy fifth, the figure is around four out of ten. And the difference has grown. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discovery of chicken immune cells could pave the way for more effective poultry vaccines
item.description: A previously unknown population of immune cells in chickens has been discovered by researchers from the University of Bristol Veterinary School in collaboration with The Pirbright Institute. The finding could help transform the way poultry vaccines are developed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New 'hunter-killer' chemistry captures and destroys forever chemicals
item.description: They can turn up in a nonstick frying pan, a waterproof jacket, a takeout food wrapper or the foam used to fight fires. Known as "forever chemicals," these substances are ubiquitous in modern society, prized for their extreme durability and versatility. However, their charm comes with a curse: They are so durable they resist degradation, posing threats to human health and the environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smart farming is already proving profitable in some regions, global analysis finds
item.description: The use of robots, drones and AI tools in agriculture is already paying off on 42% of the world's cropland. This could increase to 50% in the next 20 years and to as much as 75% if every country tightened environmental regulations. If every country loosened its regulations, it would fall to 31%. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Survey experiment shows investors focus on type of business rather than gender of leaders
item.description: Would you prefer to back a man or a woman pitching a business idea? A new study by the University of Portsmouth published in the British Journal of Management suggests that, when it comes to potential crowdfunding investors, the answer may depend less on who is pitching and more on what they are selling. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Auroral structure could be caused by bouncing electrons
item.description: The aurora is among nature's most visually striking phenomena. It occurs when charged particles from the sun are funneled by Earth's magnetic field into the upper atmosphere, where they collide with atoms and molecules and produce distinctly colored curtainlike patterns of light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experimental Facilities
item.description: Research teams at the NASA Glenn Research Center perform experiments in world-class facilities such as the 9- by 15-Foot Low-Speed Wind Tunnel (9 x15 LSWT), the Aero-Acoustic Propulsion Laboratory (AAPL), the Small Hot Jet Acoustic Rig (SHJAR), the Nozzle Acoustic Test Rig (NATR), the DGEN AeroPropulsion Research Turbofan (DART), and the Acoustical Testing Laboratory (ATL). […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA’s Simulated Mars Crew Marks One Year Inside Habitat
item.description: The four crew members in NASA’s simulated Mars mission have spent the past year living and working in isolation in a confined habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Abby Graf

item.title: Advice around children's screen use can be overwhelming. There is no single 'right' approach
item.description: When should your child start engaging with screens? How long should they use them for? Can they watch or play alone? Should there be a gap before bed? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Many data centers are located where water resources are limited
item.description: One-quarter of the world's data centers are located in areas where water demand exceeds supply for at least one month each year, according to a new global analysis. Researchers reporting in Environmental Science & Technology mapped data center locations against available water resources and found that, under a future climate scenario, the proportion of facilities in water-stressed areas could rise to one-third. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beyond the screen: E-health literacy steers young adults to professional health care
item.description: Better electronic health (e-health) literacy encourages young adult patients to visit doctors' offices rather than replace professional consultations with self-treatment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's core may have been leaking hydrogen for billions of years
item.description: When Earth formed billions of years ago, its metallic core was wrapped in a global ocean of molten rock, which eventually cooled and crystallized to form the mantle. Today, when deep-rooted mantle plumes rise toward the surface and produce volcanic eruptions, the resulting lava can contain hydrogen from deep inside the planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists redetermine a key strontium frequency with 50 times better precision for quantum technologies
item.description: The Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) has remeasured a key transition frequency of the strontium (Sr) atom for the first time in 88 years, since 1938, using a photonic grating chip. It has established a new absolute frequency value with a measurement uncertainty reduced by more than 50 times. By providing an accurate reference value for next-generation quantum technologies, this achievement is expected to contribute to the precise control and miniaturization of quantum devices, including atomic clocks and neutral-atom quantum computers. The work is published in the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Euclid discovers its first new comet 810 million miles from Earth
item.description: The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet in images taken between Sept. 16 and 24, 2026. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How do people quickly recognize what others may be feeling?
item.description: Communicating effectively with others involves recognizing emotions from faces and voices. How does the brain process and integrate emotional information from what others show and say? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Oldest animals on Earth found to share a common wormlike ancestor
item.description: New research from the University of St Andrews has shed light on the evolution of an important yet thus far poorly understood group of marine invertebrate animals—brachiopods. The work, published in Science Advances, presents the first comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of all five extant brachiopod orders and related lineages. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why the ugly history of IQ testing matters for AI and education
item.description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has recently been discussing "artificial general intelligence" that matches or surpasses human capabilities. This is from the same person who has said children born today (including his own) will "never be more intelligent than AI, from a 'raw IQ'" (intelligence quotient) perspective. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI reads centuries-old handwriting to reveal Britain's vast historic shipping trade
item.description: Historians have created a first-of-its-kind online interactive map, using data from hundreds of thousands of pages of centuries-old port records to chart Britain's growth into a dominant global trading nation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient technique can improve the bland taste of beans
item.description: Faba beans are rich in protein and can easily be grown in Denmark—yet they are more often used as animal feed than as food for people. One of the main reasons is that their flavor does not meet consumer expectations compared with beef, pork or chicken. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Giving AI a 'crystal clear' view of the materials world by mapping geometry to text
item.description: In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them the perfect material for the job. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: '24/7 unmanned synthesis platform' uses robots and light to produce drug candidates
item.description: Even when AI designs molecules with potential as medicines, drug development can be delayed if the process of producing them is slow. KAIST researchers have developed an "unmanned synthesis platform" that uses synthesis robots and light to automatically carry out the entire process from mixing raw materials to synthesis and analysis. The technology is expected to help secure a wider range of drug candidate compounds by reducing the burden of repetitive experiments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers use artificial intelligence to design potential antiviral compounds
item.description: Viral infections can be difficult to treat because viruses evolve rapidly, allowing them to develop resistance to drugs designed to attack viral proteins directly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Context is key in how people understand language
item.description: When describing someone running, most people would say exactly that: "The person is running." They probably wouldn't say the person is moving, even though both descriptions are technically correct. But what if that person were the only one moving in a room full of people standing still? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-rays reveal surprisingly long-lived spin waves in copper oxide
item.description: Today's computer technology, based on silicon chips, is slowly reaching its physical limits. Components cannot be miniaturized indefinitely, and clock speeds cannot be increased indefinitely. At the same time, huge AI data centers are being built in many places, and these consume an immense amount of electricity. This is why scientists around the world are searching for novel materials that can replace or complement silicon technology and consume significantly less electricity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UN climate panel head wants swift end to deadlock over key scientific report
item.description: The world's top climate scientists will reconvene at the earliest opportunity, the panel's chair said on Monday, after member states failed to agree when to release its crucial new findings on global heating. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Imagine a social media algorithm that prioritizes trust over outrage
item.description: Following Ukraine's recent drone strikes on Russian data centers, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of fewer Kremlin-linked bot networks spreading misinformation and disinformation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
item.description: At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days. Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Object thought to be Amelia Earhart’s missing plane likely just 'large trees', researchers find
item.description: An expedition to investigate if an anomaly seen on a satellite image of a remote island in the South Pacific was Amelia Earhart’s missing plane has ended without recovering the wreckage. Fuente: Sky News - World.

item.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
item.description: All the evidence points to the debris being part of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket. Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.description: La Agencia Espacial Japonesa, JAXA, lanzará hoy rumbo a Marte una de sus misiones más ambiciosas: MMX (Martian Moons eXploration). Como su propio nombre en inglés indica, su objetivo será estudiar las dos lunas de Marte, Deimos y Fobos. No será la primera misión que lo haga, pero sí la primera que, si todo va bien, traerá muestras de una de ellas de vuelta a la Tierra. Con misiones como las chinas Chang’e , que han traído muestras desde la Luna, hemos visto la importancia de poder analizar directamente aquí abajo el material recogido más allá de nuestro planeta. item.description: La misión, cuyo lanzamiento está previsto para el lunes, se dirige a Fobos, la mayor de las dos lunas de Marte. Podría traer de vuelta las primeras muestras del sistema marciano. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.

item.title: Cómo es la revolucionaria misión que busca traer un trozo de la mayor luna de Marte a la Tierra
item.description: La misión espacial japonesa MMX tiene la ambiciosa misión de traer 10 gramos de polvo lunar marciano de vuelta a la Tierra para ser estudiado y resolver el misterio de la formación de las lunas de Marte. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
item.description: A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. As glaciers retreat, similar disasters could become a growing danger in mountainous coastal regions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Teaching financial literacy—key to preventing underinsurance
item.description: James Cook University researchers are calling for greater attention to financial literacy in schools after a new study found that people with a strong understanding of personal insurance were more likely to engage with insurance products. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
item.description: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Musk pledges to give ‘every kid in America’ one of his SpaceX shares
item.description: Tech billionaire Elon Musk said on Monday that he would give every child in the United States a share in his SpaceX rocket company. “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” Musk, the richest man in the world, said on X. “This will be the first of many,” he said, without providing details about how the scheme would work. There are around 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to 2024 data from the US Census Bureau. Musk owns 38... Publicado también por: South China Morning Post. Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Sean O'Kane

item.title: Something strange is happening beneath a volcano near 2 million people
item.description: Scientists have discovered evidence of two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano, where satellite observations revealed mysterious ground movements suggesting magma is shifting deep underground. The findings could improve eruption forecasting for the active volcano, which sits near 2 million people and attracts tourists to its spectacular lava lake. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Labeling foods with added sugar content may reduce demand and consumption
item.description: The labeling of added sugar on food labels, which became mandatory in the U.S. by 2021, may reduce demand for and consumption of certain types of food, according to a study led by researchers in Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover why some people still can’t taste food after COVID-19
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a possible explanation for why some people struggle to taste food more than a year after recovering from COVID-19. By examining taste buds from patients with lingering symptoms, researchers discovered molecular abnormalities that weaken the signals responsible for detecting sweet, bitter, and savory flavors. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Genomic study uncovers a new lace bug species on Japan's remote Ogasawara Islands
item.description: Researchers have used genome-wide DNA data to identify a new insect species on the Ogasawara Islands, a remote Japanese archipelago roughly 900 to 1,000 kilometers (560 to 620 miles) south of Tokyo. The findings suggest that evolution among island insects is more intricate than appearances imply. The study is published in ZooKeys. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Euclid discovers new comet
item.description: The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, in images taken between 16 and 24 September 2026. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Japanese philosophy offers a new perspective on education
item.description: Modern education is predominantly shaped by approaches that emphasize efficiency, measurable achievement, prediction and the ability to solve problems through rational intervention. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
item.description: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers are ignoring most living things: Analysis finds vertebrates dominate biodiversity research
item.description: According to two new UNSW studies, researchers often choose research topics based on personal preferences and cultural attitudes, including exposure to films, TV shows and even zoos, rather than attempting to fill the most pressing gaps in knowledge. The studies are published in the journal Ecology and Evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
item.description: Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers advance aquifer mapping using remote sensing and statistical models to improve groundwater management
item.description: Groundwater in many areas of the U.S. and across the globe is being depleted as pumping for drinking water and agriculture outpaces nature's ability to refill aquifers. In the most severe cases, this could lead to a point of no return, where an aquifer's physical structure collapses and it cannot be refilled. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What to Know About the Search for Amelia Earhart’s Plane
item.description: A satellite image sent researchers to a remote Pacific atoll, but their findings brought no resolution to the decades-old search. Here’s what to know. Fuente: The New York Times - World.
item.dc:creator: Jin Yu Young

item.title: Astronomers discover a ghostly green star unlike any known before
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered a surprising rainbow of dead stars, including the first known star that would appear genuinely green to human eyes. Researchers found that white dwarfs can glow in unexpected shades of pink, purple, yellow, and cyan because of unusual chemical interactions in their extremely dense atmospheres. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
item.description: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nations seek reset at UN talks as nature goals off track
item.description: Nearly 200 nations are gathering in Armenia on Monday for critical negotiations as governments come under pressure to salvage a landmark nature pact whose goals are slipping out of reach. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The painstaking task of cataloging the world's species
item.description: A bumblebee-like insect that was last seen in France 150 years ago was spotted again in the Paris region in 2025. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
item.description: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
item.description: Researchers travelled to a remote Pacific Island to confirm whether an object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the mystery of the pilot's disappearance. Fuente: BBC News - World.

item.title: Factoring daily weather extremes into glacier models reveals greater ice loss and faster sea-level rise
item.description: A new study led by researchers at ETH Zurich (Switzerland) and the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) reveals that glaciers worldwide could lose ice faster than previously projected. Published in Nature Communications, the research shows that accounting for daily weather variability leads to more realistic simulations of glacier melt and results in greater projected ice loss by the end of the century. The findings highlight the importance of short-lived weather events, such as the exceptional heat waves and extreme melt seasons recently observed in several glacierized regions around the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: On the front line of ocean conservation off Portugal's Madeira
item.description: Juan Mayorga smiled as a stingray glided across his computer screen, moving gracefully over the seabed near Portugal's Desertas Islands, part of the Madeira archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En Sevilla alguien ha tirado un fusil de asalto y un posible lanzagranadas a la basura. Ahora la Policía busca al dueño
item.description: ¿Te imaginas estar paseando al perro y ver como alguien lanza por la ventanilla del coche un lanzacohetes, conduciendo en dirección contraria, y se pierde entre el tráfico? No es una escena de Grand Theft Auto VI, es algo que ha pasado en Sevilla. Una bolsa de basura negra, en mitad de una calle de un barrio residencial de Sevilla, y de ella asomando algo que no suele aparecer entre los desperdicios: un fusil de asalto y un tubo que podría ser un lanzagranadas. Es lo que se encontró una vecina del Tiro de Línea el pasado miércoles 14 de octubre. Su foto circuló después por redes y desató… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Isra Fdez

item.title: Record El Niño? Depends who's counting
item.description: Britain's Met Office says this year's El Niño is "unprecedented." Japan's weather agency has called it the strongest ever observed. U.S. forecasters say it still trails the biggest events in its record books. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ISS mission: 'It's really exciting to see this renewal of French women in space'
item.description: More than six decades after thirteen pioneering women demonstrated they could meet the same demanding physical tests as America's first male astronauts, gender equality in space exploration remains an unfinished journey, explains Laurène Delsupexhe, Chemical Propulsion Engineer at the European Space Agency. From the institutional exclusion of the Mercury 13 to the renewed ambitions of NASA's Artemis programme, Delsupexhe traces the remarkable progress of women in space while exposing the persistent barriers that have outlasted generations of scientific and technological breakthroughs. With… Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees
item.description: Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees. “Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok

item.title: Having a baby is too expensive, 4 in 5 parents say
item.description: Welcoming a new baby brings moments of joy, major milestones and significant expenses. And four in five parents say it costs too much to have a baby, according to the University of Michigan Health C.S. Mott Children's Hospital National Poll on Children's Health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Fall color covers the forested slopes of Bieszczady National Park, while patches of polonina, a type of high-mountain meadow, have turned tan. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Fatty liver disease is actually five different conditions, scientists discover
item.description: A common liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide may be far more complicated than scientists previously realized. Mayo Clinic researchers have discovered that fatty liver disease actually consists of five distinct biological subtypes, each carrying different risks for liver failure, cancer, heart disease, and other serious complications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: Researchers have found that tornado activity has shifted eastward in the United States in recent years. Here’s what experts recommend to stay safe: WASHINGTONPOST.COM More tornadoes are popping up in Eastern cities. Here’s how to stay safe. Fuente: The Washington Post.

item.title: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
item.description: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Who's paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom (or bubble)
item.description: Imagine a company that sells you equipment, invests money in your business and then rents back what you build with it. It's your supplier, your investor and your customer all at once. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Early humans in America endured climate chaos—new research
item.description: Some 23,000 years ago, during the coldest part of the last ice age, people walked across the muddy margins of an ancient lake in what is now White Sands National Park, New Mexico. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's oldest evidence of life is written in stone—but it's at risk of disappearing
item.description: Today, our planet is teeming with life, but it has not always looked the same. Long before forests reached skyward, animals walked on land and dinosaurs rose and fell, our planet was shaped by a much smaller, more unassuming form of life. And we can still find traces of it today. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars' moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spatial genomics tool maps long-range DNA interactions while preserving cells' locations within tissues
item.description: DNA is not randomly distributed within the nucleus but is packaged with proteins into chromatin, which is precisely folded into complex three-dimensional structures. However, scientists have not fully understood how this complex three-dimensional (3D) organization is regulated or how it changes over time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2023, California moved 246 endangered abalone; by 2026, counts rose from 54 to 302, with juveniles found
item.description: In 2023, researchers relocated 246 black abalone to a protected coastal site to encourage population growth. After three years, surveys recorded an increase in individuals from 54 to 302, showing signs of recovery. Juvenile abalone were also found, which raises hopes for future reproduction. This project involved collaboration among several scientific organizations and demonstrated the feasibility of habitat restoration. Ongoing monitoring will be crucial to determine the population's long-term sustainability. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: New monolithic ion trap opens quantum simulations to more researchers
item.description: Some quantum systems are so complex that even the most powerful supercomputers struggle to simulate their behavior. One solution is quantum simulation: building a controllable quantum system in the lab and tuning it to mimic the one researchers want to understand. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new way to detect stabilizing properties of optical devices
item.description: In optical fibers, chips and other light-guiding devices, minor defects can scatter photons and disrupt their path. A new study demonstrates a way to reveal properties which, in certain systems, help light wave behavior withstand such flaws. The method could help speed up the search for new kinds of electronics and optical technologies, and contribute to more reliable quantum devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists prove a long-suspected quantum speed limit for thermalization
item.description: Whether we are waiting for a car windshield to defrost in winter or a warm drink to cool down, how long it takes for an object to settle into a stable, even temperature within its environment (thermal equilibrium) depends on numerous factors. These can include surface area, the material properties of an object and airflow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genome detectives: Researchers sequence the genome of a harmful plant pathogen
item.description: Graduate students in Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences contributed to the first complete genome sequence of a harmful plant pathogen from an ornamental Prunus host through an active-learning activity in a plant disease diagnosis course. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a way to reverse coral bleaching at record speed
item.description: For the first time, scientists have observed bleached corals on the brink of death fully recover through brief contact with healthy clones. Ghostly white corals returned to full health in a laboratory setting within seven weeks, the fastest documented recovery to date, according to a study published in Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Close social relationships are known to contribute to the survival of many animals, including humans. Maintaining social bonds over time, however, can also require effort and sacrifices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan's MMX mission aims to swipe soil samples from Mars's moon Phobos
item.description: A Japanese space mission is about to launch towards Mars. But it will not land on the planet itself. Instead, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission will focus on Phobos, the bigger of Mars's two small moons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a natural compound that could protect the brain from too much salt
item.description: Eating too much salt may do more than raise blood pressure. It could also harm memory and social behavior. In a new study, Japanese researchers discovered that a soy-derived compound called LPC70 helped protect mice from several damaging effects of a high-salt diet. Mice given the supplement had lower blood pressure, better memory, and improved social interactions compared with mice consuming excess salt alone. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
item.description: Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions." Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
item.description: Eating blueberries every day could have surprising effects on mood, according to a small study that found greater reductions in depressive symptoms among older adults who consumed the fruit for three months. Researchers also detected changes in gut microbial enzymes, suggesting a possible gut-brain connection, although the mood benefits were not statistically significant compared with a placebo. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
